title: Energy stores and transfers
description: Animated KS3 Physics lesson on energy for ages 9 to 14: energy stores, energy transfers, conservation of energy, useful and wasted energy, efficiency, and renewable and non-renewable energy resources.
intro: Where energy is stored, how it moves, why it is never used up, efficiency and energy resources, explained by the owl in five short parts.

steps.say: Energy makes things happen. We measure energy in **joules**. The short way to write joules is **J**.
steps.speak: Energy makes things happen. We measure energy in joules. The short way to write joules is J.

steps.say: Energy is kept in **stores**. Food, fuels and batteries have energy in a **chemical store**.
Anything that is moving has energy in its **kinetic store**. The faster it goes, the more energy.
Anything lifted up high has energy in its **gravitational store**. The higher it is, the more energy.
Stretched or squashed things, like a rubber band or a spring, have energy in an **elastic store**.
Hot things have more energy in their **thermal store** than cold things. There are a few more stores too, like **magnetic** and **nuclear**.

check.q: A skier stands still at the top of a high mountain. Which store has lots of energy because of her height?
check.hint: She isn't moving yet, so it can't be the store for moving things. Which store is about being high up?
check.explain: Things that are high up have energy in their **gravitational store**. She is standing still, so her kinetic store is empty until she starts to ski down.

steps.say: Energy can move from one store to another. This is called an **energy transfer**.
A ball falls off a shelf. It gets lower, so its gravitational store empties. It gets faster, so its kinetic store fills up.
Energy is transferred in four main ways: by a **force** (mechanically), **electrically**, by **heating**, and by **light** and **sound**.
A torch: the battery's chemical store is transferred electrically to the bulb. The bulb gives out light, and it also heats the surroundings a little.

check.q: You wind up a toy car, then let it go and it speeds off. The energy is transferred from…
options: the elastic store to the kinetic store
the kinetic store to the elastic store
the chemical store to the kinetic store
the gravitational store to the elastic store
check.hint: Winding it up squashes a spring inside. What does the car do when you let go?
check.explain: Winding it squashes a spring, filling its **elastic store**. When you let go, the spring unwinds and the car speeds up, so the energy goes to the **kinetic store**.

steps.say: Here is a very important rule: energy cannot be **created** or **destroyed**. It can only be transferred.
An old filament light bulb is given 100 J of energy electrically. 20 J comes out as light. 80 J heats the room.
steps.speak: An old filament light bulb is given 100 joules of energy electrically. 20 joules comes out as light. 80 joules heats the room.

steps.say: 20 J + 80 J = 100 J. All the energy is still there. None of it has vanished.
steps.speak: 20 joules plus 80 joules equals 100 joules. All the energy is still there. None of it has vanished.

steps.say: The light is the **useful** energy. The heating is **wasted** energy. Wasted energy spreads out and warms the surroundings a tiny bit. We say it is **dissipated**.
We can waste less energy. Oil on a bike chain cuts friction, so less energy is wasted heating the chain.

check.q: A motor is given 200 J of energy. 150 J goes usefully into the kinetic store. How much energy is wasted?
check.hint: Energy is not destroyed. Energy in = useful energy + wasted energy. What do you add to 150 J to make 200 J?
check.explain: 200 J − 150 J = **50 J** is wasted, mostly heating the motor and the air around it. It is not destroyed, just not useful.

steps.say: **Efficiency** tells you how much of the energy put in is useful. Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in.
steps.speak: Efficiency tells you how much of the energy put in is useful. Efficiency equals useful energy out, divided by total energy in.

steps.say: For the filament bulb: 20 J ÷ 100 J = 0.2. As a percentage that is 20%. Only 20% of the energy is useful.
steps.speak: For the filament bulb: 20 joules divided by 100 joules is 0.2. As a percentage that is 20 percent. Only 20 percent of the energy is useful.

steps.say: An electric motor is given 100 J and 80 J goes into its kinetic store. Its efficiency is 80 ÷ 100 = 80%.
steps.speak: An electric motor is given 100 joules and 80 joules goes into its kinetic store. Its efficiency is 80 divided by 100, which is 80 percent.

steps.say: LED bulbs waste much less energy heating the room than filament bulbs, so they are much more **efficient**.
No device can be more than 100% efficient. You can never get out more energy than you put in.
steps.speak: No device can be more than 100 percent efficient. You can never get out more energy than you put in.

check.q: A kettle is given 1000 J of energy. 800 J heats the water. What is its efficiency?
check.hint: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in. Which energy is useful for a kettle?
check.explain: Heating the water is useful. 800 ÷ 1000 = 0.8, which is **80%**. (20% is the part that is wasted.)

steps.say: We need **energy resources** to make electricity, heat our homes and move cars, buses and planes.
**Coal**, **oil** and **natural gas** are **fossil fuels**. They formed from plants and animals over millions of years. They are **non-renewable**: one day they will run out.
Burning fossil fuels gives out **carbon dioxide**. This gas traps heat in the air, which adds to **global warming**.
**Renewable** resources will not run out: wind, solar (sunlight), hydroelectric (falling water), tides, waves and **geothermal** (heat from hot rocks underground).
But wind and solar depend on the weather. No wind, no spin. At night, no sunlight. Geothermal works in any weather.

check.q: Why are coal, oil and natural gas called **non-renewable**?
options: They took millions of years to form, so they will run out
They only work when it is windy or sunny
They do not give out carbon dioxide
They cannot be used to make electricity
check.hint: Renewable means it can be replaced as fast as we use it. Can we make more coal quickly?
check.explain: Fossil fuels took **millions of years** to form. We are using them far faster than that, so once they are burned they are gone: they will run out.
